==Description==
'''''Peucedanum officinale''''' is a herbaceous [[perennial plant]] in the family [[Apiaceae]] found mainly in Central Europe and Southern Europe.<ref>''Flowers of Europe,a Field Guide'' [[Oleg Polunin]], Oxford University Press 1969</ref>
It is also native to the UK, where it has the common names '''hog's fennel'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''sulphurweed''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=6 November 2014}}</ref> but it is a rare plant there, occurring only in certain localities in the counties of [[Essex]] and [[Kent]]. It was formerly also found near the town of [[Shoreham-by-Sea]] in the county of [[West Sussex]], but has long been [[extinct]] there.

==Habitat==
Rough [[grassland]], clayey banks and cliffs near the sea. It is a [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] perennial with stems up to 2 m in height, solid, [[striate]], sometimes weakly angled, sparsely blotched wine red, surrounded by fibrous remains of [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s at the base and springing from a stout [[rootstock]]. The [[umbel]]s of greenish-yellow flowers contrast pleasingly with the bushy, radiating mass of dark green, long-petioled leaves, which bear [[linear]], [[sessility (botany)|sessile]] lobes, [[Leaf shape|attenuate]] at both ends and having narrow, cartilaginous margins (i.e., individual lobes resembling blades of grass).<ref>''Umbellifers of the British Isles'' Tutin T.G. BSBI Handbook No.2. Pub. Botanical Society of the British Isles, 1980.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Peucedanum officinale'' has been known as a medicinal plant in Britain since at least the 17th century and features in the [[herbals]] of [[Nicholas Culpeper]] (in whose day it was more plentiful, for he records it as growing abundantly on [[Faversham]] marshes) and [[John Gerard]]. Culpepper records the additional common names '''hoar strange, hoar strong''', (compare German "Haarstrang", meaning ''hog's tail'') '''brimstonewort''' and '''sulphurwort'''.

The long stout taproot - 'black without and white within' and sometimes 'as big as a man's thigh', as Gerard has it - yields, when incised in Spring, a considerable quantity of a yellowish-green [[latex]], which dries into a gummy [[oleoresin]] and retains the strong, sulphurous scent of the root. This harvesting technique, and the product so obtained, very much recall those of two other medicinal [[umbellifers]]: ''[[Ferula assa-foetida]]'' and ''[[Dorema ammoniacum]]''.<ref>''A Modern Herbal'' Grieve,M.,Pub.1931,Jonathan Cape Ltd.,reprinted 1974 and 1975.</ref><ref>''The Englishman's Flora'',Grigson,G.,Pub. Readers Union Phoenix House Ltd.,London 1958.</ref> A decoction of the root of ''P. officinale'' is [[diuretic]], [[sudorific]], [[antiscorbutic]] and controls [[menstruation]]. ''Gummi Peucedani'', the oleoresin derived from the drying of the root latex, has properties similar to those of ''Gum Ammoniac'' (the oleoresin derived from ''Dorema ammoniacum''). ''Peucedanum officinale'' has also been used in [[veterinary medicine]].<ref>''A Dictionary of Plants Used by Man'' Usher, George. Pub. Constable, London 1974.</ref>
